newsitem.title: UK: Market valuation fears prompt fund focus on cash.
newsitem.headline: Market valuation fears prompt fund focus on cash.

text.p: The unnerving rise in global equity markets and low yields in major bond markets have pushed some fund managers into raising cash holdings ahead of a potential market reversal.
They said the search for value was becoming increasingly difficult, and fears of a pullback in key markets had put some major players on the defensive.
"Cash is not pre-eminently desirable, it is not utterly essential. But is it sensible? That is a different story," said Nick Knight, global strategist at Nomura International.
Some recent asset allocation switches in the UK have highlighted the concern about a reversal.

Standard Life said it had moved some 400 million sterling out of equities into cash in recent weeks, and Scottish Widows Investment Management said it had sold about 250 million sterling of its European equity holdings and moved the funds into gilts.
"The money has been invested in gilts because SWIM could not find enough attraction in any other equity market," said global strategist Robin Garrow.
Garrow expects a U.S.-led correction in world markets of the order of 15-20 percent in the next six to 12 months.
Standard's chief investment manager, Sandy Crombie, has predicted there will be a correction of up to 15 percent in the market in the next three to six months.
PDFM has long held the view that the market is due for a fall and has built a 10 billion sterling cash holding.
But many fund are maintaining the view that valuations have further to go, saying the market has entered a new phase where it will not be subject to the boom-bust cycles of old.
Nomura's Knight said that the valuations were historically expensive, but may not be if current benign conditions remained in place.
"In 20 years' time we may look back at the discontinuity of valuations that occurred in the early nineties as a function of the final acceptance of a low inflation high-growth semi-permanent state.
"We'll laugh at how we thought 20 times earnings was expensive," he said.
Scudder, Stevens & Clark, which had been running a high cash weighting in its global equity portfolio, has recently scaled back that position.
Spokeswoman Jenny Brundit told Reuters the high cash weighting had been run as the firm scratched for fresh value.
"Valuations are high at the moment so we are taking extra time to seek out value because there is just very high value globally, not only in the States but also in Europe."
Scudder's cash position has come down to about 9.5 percent from 15 to 16 percent.
"We are not going to sit it out, we are just going to seek out good values," she said, pointing to health and technology sectors as current favourites.

In fixed income, she said UK bonds had been offering the best value recently. It is a view shared by Knight, who said the UK bond market was one of the few that hadn't taken on board the benign inflation outlook.
"The UK bond market has not really taken on the full paradigm shift in inflation, potentially. But other than that there is no value."
But the concerns about a correction in the market have to be weighed against the potential for missing a big extension of the recent rally.

"No-one is pretending this is an earnings-driven market or that it is cheap. It is a liquidity-driven market and that is a difficult tape to fight but sensible people who have been around the track will probably sell into it a bit," said Knight.

A study of UK pooled pension fund performances showed that some of the top fund managers in London had substantially underperformed their peers so far in 1997 -- partly due to high cash weightings and below average allocations to the top performing U.S. and European equity markets.
A Reuter asset allocation survey in July showed UK pension funds were raising cash weightings, while global equity and bond portfolios were running relatively high cash positions.
